'''''Howea belmoreana''''', the '''curly palm''', '''kentia palm''', or '''Belmore sentry palm''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Arecaceae]], [[endemic species|endemic]] to [[Lord Howe Island]], Australia. It and ''[[Howea forsteriana]]'' probably evolved from a common ancestor through [[sympatric speciation]].<ref>[http://www.the-scientist.com/news/display/23103/ ''Evidence for sympatric speciation''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071024124130/http://www.the-scientist.com/news/display/23103/ |date=24 October 2007 }} The Scientist, Stuart Blackman, 9 February 2006</ref> The canopy of a mature kentia palm tree spreads {{convert|5|-|10|ft|m|0|abbr=on}} in diameter and contains roughly 36 leaves.<ref>{{cite web | title = Real Palm Trees | website = Palm Tree General Description | url =http://realpalmtrees.com/palm-blog/k-o/kentia-palm-howea-forsteriana/}}</ref>

''Howea belmoreana'' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=''Howea belmoreana'' AGM|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=6330|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=23 July 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 50 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 7 March 2018}}</ref>

== Effects of mycorrhiza on speciation ==
''Howea belmoreana'' is restricted to the volcanic soils on Lord Howe Island, whereas ''H. forsteriana'' is found on both alkaline [[calcareous]] and volcanic soils, the two most common soil types found on the island. ''Howea belmoreana'' is more common on volcanic soils and has a higher survival rate than ''H. forsteriana''.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hipperson H, Dunning LT, Baker WJ, Butlin RK, Hutton I, Papadopulos AS, Smadja CM, Wilson TC, Devaux C, Savolainen V | display-authors = 6 | title = Ecological speciation in sympatric palms: 2. Pre- and post-zygotic isolation | journal = Journal of Evolutionary Biology | volume = 29 | issue = 11 | pages = 2143–2156 | date = November 2016 | pmid = 27374779 | pmc = 5096058 | doi = 10.1111/jeb.12933 }}</ref> Osborne et al. (2018) suggest that the speciation of ''H. forsteriana'' and ''Howea belmoreana'' is partially a result of difference in [[arbuscular mycorrhiza]] based on soil types. The levels of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi were significantly lower in the roots of ''Howea forsteriana'' on volcanic soil, compared to the same species on calcareous soil and to ''Howea belmoreana'' on the same volcanic soil. The symbiotic relationship between the plant and the fungi exchanges carbons from the plant for essential nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphate that would be otherwise inaccessible to the plant. The decreased fungal relationships in ''Howea forsteriana'' in volcanic soil may disadvantage it compared to ''Howea belmoreana''.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Osborne OG, De-Kayne R, Bidartondo MI, Hutton I, Baker WJ, Turnbull CG, Savolainen V|author7-link=Vincent Savolainen | title = Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi promote coexistence and niche divergence of sympatric palm species on a remote oceanic island | journal = The New Phytologist | volume = 217 | issue = 3 | pages = 1254–1266 | date = February 2018 | pmid = 29034978 | pmc = 5813143 | doi = 10.1111/nph.14850 }}</ref>
